title: Stimulated Emission
short_intro: Stimulated emission is a quantum process in which an incoming photon of specific energy interacts with an excited atom, triggering it to drop to a lower energy state and emit a second photon identical in phase, frequency, direction, and polarization. It forms the foundational physical principle behind laser action and light amplification.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic understanding of absorption, spontaneous emission, and stimulated emission, along with Einstein's A and B coefficients and their qualitative relations.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed mathematical formulation of Einstein's relations, thermal equilibrium derivation of population inversion requirements, and threshold conditions for laser operation.

prerequisites: Bohr's atomic model and discrete energy states
Planck's radiation law and thermal equilibrium

concept_notes.heading: Fundamental Interaction Processes
bullets: Absorption involves an electron in a lower energy state E<sub>1</sub> absorbing an incident photon of energy hν = E<sub>2</sub> - E<sub>1</sub> and transitioning to the excited state E<sub>2</sub>.

Spontaneous emission is the random decay of an electron from the excited state E<sub>2</sub> to E<sub>1</sub> without external stimulation, emitting an incoherent photon with random phase and direction.
Stimulated emission requires an incoming photon of exact energy hν = E<sub>2</sub> - E<sub>1</sub> to induce an excited electron to drop to E<sub>1</sub>, releasing a clone photon.

concept_notes.heading: Characteristics of Stimulated Photons
bullets: Coherence: The emitted photon is exactly in phase with the stimulating photon, maintaining spatial and temporal coherence.
Monochromaticity: The frequency of the emitted photon strictly matches the frequency of the incident photon, ν = (E<sub>2</sub> - E<sub>1</sub>)/h.
Directionality: The secondary photon travels in the precise geometrical direction of the primary stimulating photon, yielding a highly collimated beam.

concept_notes.heading: Einstein's Coefficients
bullets: A<sub>21</sub> represents the Einstein coefficient for spontaneous emission, signifying the probability per unit time that an atom in state 2 decays to state 1.
B<sub>21</sub> represents the Einstein coefficient for stimulated emission, governing the transition rate from state 2 to state 1 induced by radiation density ρ(ν).
B<sub>12</sub> represents the Einstein coefficient for induced absorption, governing the upward transition rate from state 1 to state 2.

concept_notes.heading: Condition for Amplification and Population Inversion
bullets: Under normal thermal equilibrium, the lower state population N<sub>1</sub> exceeds the upper state population N<sub>2</sub> according to the Boltzmann factor.
For light amplification via stimulated emission to dominate over absorption, the condition N<sub>2</sub> > N<sub>1</sub> must be satisfied, known as population inversion.
An external energy source called a 'pump' is required to achieve and maintain population inversion against natural decay rates.

derivations.title: Derivation of Einstein's Relations between A and B Coefficients
derivations.conditions: System of atoms in thermal equilibrium with radiation of energy density ρ(ν) at temperature T.
steps: Write the rate of upward transitions (absorption): R<sub>12</sub> = N_1 B_{12} ρ(ν).
Write the total rate of downward transitions (spontaneous + stimulated): R<sub>21</sub> = N_2 [A_{21} + B_{21} ρ(ν)].
Equate upward and downward transition rates in thermal equilibrium: N_1 B_{12} ρ(ν) = N_2 [A_{21} + B_{21} ρ(ν)].
Express energy density from this balance: ρ(ν) = \frac{A_{21} / B_{21}}{(N_1 / N_2)(B_{12} / B_{21}) - 1}.
Substitute the Maxwell-Boltzmann ratio N_1 / N_2 = \frac{g_1}{g_2} \exp\left(\frac{h\nu}{k_B T}\right). Assuming g_1 = g_2 = 1, N_1 / N_2 = \exp\left(\frac{h\nu}{k_B T}\right).
Compare the resulting expression with Planck's Radiation Law: ρ(ν) = \frac{8\pi h \nu^3}{c^3} \frac{1}{\exp(h\nu / k_B T) - 1}.
Equating coefficients yields B_{12} = B_{21} and \frac{A_{21}}{B_{21}} = \frac{8\pi h \nu^3}{c^3}.

derivations.title: Ratio of Spontaneous to Stimulated Emission Probabilities
derivations.conditions: Harmonic radiation field in an optical cavity at frequency ν.
steps: Define the ratio of spontaneous emission rate to stimulated emission rate as R = \frac{A_{21}}{B_{21} \rho(\nu)}.
Substitute Planck's expression for energy density ρ(ν) = \frac{8\pi h \nu^3}{c^3} \frac{1}{\exp(h\nu / k_B T) - 1}.
Substitute the relation A_{21} / B_{21} = \frac{8\pi h \nu^3}{c^3}.
Simplify the resulting algebraic fraction to isolate the exponential temperature dependence term.

formula_sheet.conditions: Optical and UV frequencies where h\nu \gg k_B T

graphs_and_experiments.title: Three-Level Laser Pumping Scheme Energy Diagram
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Three horizontal lines representing E_1 (ground state), E_2 (metastable state), and E_3 (pump band), with upward arrows for optical pumping, non-radiative decay from E_3 to E_2, and downward laser transition from E_2 to E_1.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how atoms are pumped to a short-lived upper band from where they decay rapidly to a metastable intermediate state, facilitating population inversion relative to the ground state.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via conceptual labeling questions in PGT physics regarding ruby laser mechanics.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Wavelength Dependence of Spontaneous vs Stimulated Emission
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A log-scale plot showing the ratio of spontaneous to stimulated emission rates increasing sharply as frequency ν increases in the optical domain.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates why achieving stimulated emission and laser action is significantly more difficult at shorter wavelengths (X-rays/UV) compared to microwaves and infrared (masers).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Explains frequency limits of lasers and conceptual constraints in high-energy photon amplification.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Boltzmann Population Distribution Curve across Thermal States
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Exponential decay curve of population N vs Energy E for different absolute temperatures T_1 and T_2.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that under thermal equilibrium, higher energy states are always less populated than lower energy states, proving that external pumping is mandatory to invert populations.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct application in numericals calculating temperature or population ratios.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the ratio of the rate of spontaneous emission to the rate of stimulated emission for a system operating at wavelength λ = 500 nm at room temperature T = 300 K. (Take h = 6.63 × 10^{-34} J s, c = 3 × 10^8 m/s, k_B = 1.38 × 10^{-23} J/K)
solution_steps: Calculate the exponent term hν / (k_B T) = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 6 \times 10^{14}}{1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300} = \frac{3.978 \times 10^{-19}}{4.14 \times 10^{-21}} \approx 96.08.
Evaluate the ratio R_spont / R_stim = \exp(h\nu / k_B T) - 1 = \exp(96.08) - 1.
solved_numericals.answer: \approx \exp(96.08) (extremely large, showing spontaneous emission completely dominates at optical wavelengths at room temperature).

solved_numericals.question: Given that the Einstein A coefficient for a certain atomic transition is 2.5 × 10^7 s^{-1} and the transition wavelength is 6000 Å, calculate the Einstein B coefficient for stimulated emission. (h = 6.63 × 10^{-34} J s, c = 3 × 10^8 m/s)
solution_steps: Identify the relation between coefficients: \frac{A_{21}}{B_{21}} = \frac{8\pi h \nu^3}{c^3} = \frac{8\pi h c}{\lambda^3}.
Substitute the given values: λ = 6000 Å = 6 × 10^{-7} m, A_{21} = 2.5 × 10^7 s^{-1}.

solved_numericals.question: At what temperature would the rate of spontaneous emission equal the rate of stimulated emission for a radiation wavelength of 1.0 μm? (h = 6.63 × 10^{-34} J s, c = 3 × 10^8 m/s, k_B = 1.38 × 10^{-23} J/K)
solution_steps: Set the ratio equal to 1: \exp(h\nu / k_B T) - 1 = 1, which means \exp(h\nu / k_B T) = 2.
Take natural logarithm on both sides: \frac{h\nu}{k_B T} = \ln 2 \approx 0.693.
Isolate temperature T: T = \frac{h c}{\lambda k_B \ln 2}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes two-level or simple multi-level atomic systems interacting with isotropic blackbody radiation fields in thermal equilibrium derivations.
Neglects Doppler broadening and collision broadening effects when defining monochromatic transition frequencies in ideal derivations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Stimulated emission produces photons of higher energy than the incident photon.
common_misconceptions.correct: Stimulated emission produces a photon with exactly the same energy (frequency) as the incident photon.
common_misconceptions.why: Energy conservation dictates that the emitted photon energy equals the exact energy difference E_2 - E_1 between the discrete atomic states.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Einstein's coefficient B_{12} is greater than B_{21} for non-degenerate systems.
common_misconceptions.correct: For non-degenerate energy levels, B_{12} equals B_{21}.
common_misconceptions.why: Microscopic reversibility and thermal equilibrium proofs establish identical transition probability magnitudes for absorption and stimulated emission.

quick_revision: Stimulated emission yields coherent, monochromatic, and directionally aligned photons triggered by an incident photon of matching energy hν = E_2 - E_1.
Rate of Induced Absorption: R_{12} = N_1 B_{12} \rho(\nu)
Rate of Spontaneous Emission: R_{spont} = N_2 A_{21}
